housing.affordability_ratio.plain: How many times the typical home's value is larger than the largest loan the typical household could carry. Above 1.0, the typical home is out of reach for the typical household under the study's method. Puerto Rico: 1.37 in the 2020-2024 window.
housing.affordability_ratio.plain_es: Cuántas veces el valor de la vivienda típica es mayor que el préstamo más grande que podría pagar el hogar típico. Por encima de 1.0, la vivienda típica está fuera del alcance del hogar típico según el método del estudio. Puerto Rico: 1.37 en la ventana 2020-2024.
housing.affordability_ratio.definition: Median home value (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25077) divided by the maximum affordable 30-year loan (calculated from median household income, ACS table B19013), for the same geography and window, rounded to two decimals.
housing.affordability_ratio.method: The observatory divides median home value by the maximum affordable loan and keeps the result only when both exist. The loan uses 30% of income for housing, 78% of that for principal and interest, a 30-year term and a fixed 5% rate. No margin of error is calculated.
housing.affordability_ratio.how_to_read: A ratio of 1.37 means the typical home is worth 37% more than the largest loan the typical household could carry. Values at or below 1.0 mean it is within reach under the method. The Housing page colors a municipality 'out of reach' when the ratio is above 1.00 and 'within reach' otherwise.
caveats: Both medians describe different groups: home value is for owner-occupied homes and owners' own estimates, while income is for all households, renters included. The ratio is a yardstick, not a measure of what buyers face for homes on the market. It does not assess whether any household can buy a home or qualify for a loan, and it is not financial advice.
It carries all the assumptions of the maximum affordable loan: 30% of income, 78% to principal and interest, a 30-year loan and a fixed 5% rate.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the ratio is above 1.0 in all 78 municipalities in every window from 2010 to 2023. In 2020-2024 it is above 1.0 in 76 of 78; Culebra (0.97) and Guayanilla (1.00) are at or below 1.0.

Near 1.0 the label is not reliable: no margin is calculated, and the ratio is rounded to two decimals before the page labels it. Guayanilla in 2020-2024 (ratio 1.00 after rounding; $87,400 value against an $87,232 maximum loan) is labeled 'within reach' although its value is slightly above the loan. In the 2026-10 snapshot, four municipalities lie between 0.95 and 1.05 in 2020-2024 (Culebra 0.97, Guayanilla 1.00, Patillas 1.01, Gurabo 1.03). Treat ratios in that range as at the line.
Value and income come from the same window, so they are in the same dollars. Small municipalities have noisy medians, and the ratio multiplies that noise; no margin is shown.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

municipalities.affordability_ratio.definition: median_home_value (table B25077 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates) divided by max_affordable_loan, from the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The ratio has no unit: it says how many times the median home value exceeds the maximum affordable loan.

The Housing page profile labels a ratio above 1.00 'out of reach' and a ratio of 1.00 or less 'within reach'. The map's Municipality tab colors the tile as a warning above 1.00 and green at 1.00 or less. Both tests use the ratio after rounding to two decimals.
municipalities.affordability_ratio.how_to_read: A ratio of 1.50 means the median home costs one and a half times the largest loan the median household could carry. A higher ratio means homes are further out of reach. It does not say how many households can buy. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write: 'Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory; calculated from US Census Bureau ACS 5-year estimates 2020-2024, tables B19013 and B25077, with the affordability method of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023).'
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 76 of 78 municipalities have a stored value above 1.00. Culebra (0.97) is below. In the same snapshot, Guayanilla is stored as 1.00, but its unrounded ratio is 1.002 (median home value $87,400, maximum loan $87,232). The map and the Housing page profile test the rounded value, so they class Guayanilla as green, or 'within reach', although its median home is $168 above its maximum loan. Treat a value near 1.00 as a tie.
It compares two medians from different groups: the value of homes that owners already hold, and the income of all households. Buyers of a home may have more or less income, savings or help.
It rests on the assumptions listed under 'Maximum affordable 30-year loan', including a fixed 5% rate and no down payment.

No margin of error is calculated for this field. Both inputs are survey estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), combining the 90% margins of the median home value and the median household income in the Housing page series with the Census Bureau's formula for the margin of a ratio (treating the two estimates as independent), the margin is larger than the distance from 1.00 in 10 of the 78 municipalities, among them Culebra, Guayanilla, Patillas, Gurabo and Vieques. For those, the survey cannot show on which side of 1.00 the true ratio lies.
An illustration of one set of assumptions across municipalities. It is not financial or lending advice and not an estimate of what any household can borrow.

housing.max_affordable_loan.plain: The largest 30-year home loan a household with the area's median income could carry. The method assumes the household spends 30% of its income on housing. About 78% of that budget goes to the loan payment, at a fixed 5% interest rate. Puerto Rico: $95,921 in the 2020-2024 window. It is a yardstick, not a lender's limit.
housing.max_affordable_loan.plain_es: El préstamo hipotecario a 30 años más grande que podría pagar un hogar con el ingreso mediano del área. El método supone que el hogar gasta 30% de su ingreso en vivienda. Cerca del 78% de ese presupuesto va al pago del préstamo, a una tasa de interés fija de 5%. Puerto Rico: $95,921 en la ventana 2020-2024. Es una referencia, no el límite de un prestamista.
housing.max_affordable_loan.definition: A calculation on median household income (American Community Survey, ACS, table B19013). Monthly housing budget = income × 0.30 / 12. Loan payment = budget × 430/549 (about 78.3%, the share of the housing budget that the study's Table 6 puts on principal and interest). Maximum loan = payment × (1 - (1 + r)^-360) / r, with r = 0.05 / 12, rounded to whole dollars.
housing.max_affordable_loan.method: The observatory applies the formula in the definition to the median household income of each municipality and of Puerto Rico in each window. The 30%, the 430/549 and the rate are fixed. The study prints no interest rate; the 5% is inferred from its Puerto Rico row (see the caveats). It is held fixed in every window, so windows differ only through incomes. No margin of error is calculated.
housing.max_affordable_loan.how_to_read: Read it as: the loan size that this method says the typical household can support. If the typical home costs more than that, the typical household is priced out under the method. It is a way to compare places and years, not a prediction of what a bank would lend. The ratio of home value to this loan is the affordability ratio.
caveats: The method makes five assumptions: 30% of income goes to housing; about 78% of that goes to principal and interest (the rest to taxes, insurance and other costs); a 30-year loan; a 5% interest rate in every window; and the median household income is the buyer's income. Change any one and the answer changes. It does not assess whether any household can buy a home or qualify for a loan, and it is not financial advice.

The study prints no interest rate. The 5% rate is inferred from the study's Puerto Rico row: $21,967 of income and an $80,181 maximum loan imply 4.994%. At exactly 5% the observatory's figures are $19 to $65 below the printed maximums.
Real mortgage rates changed over the period (the Housing page notes they ranged from under 4% to over 7%), so the figure is not what a lender would have offered in any one year.
It leaves out down payments, closing costs, other debts, credit history and lender rules. It also ignores that the median household is not necessarily a buyer.
It carries the sampling error of median household income, but no margin is shown for it.

Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window (2024 dollars for 2020-2024), as the Census Bureau states them. Amounts from different windows are not in the same dollars. To compare across windows, use the Analysis tab's Inflation-adjusted option, which restates dollars with the US Consumer Price Index (see the entry on inflation adjustment).

municipalities.max_affordable_loan.plain: This is the largest 30-year home loan that a household with the municipality's median income could carry. Three assumptions apply. Housing takes 30% of income. About 78% of that budget (23.5% of income) pays the loan. The interest rate is a fixed 5%. It is a yardstick, not a lender's limit.
municipalities.max_affordable_loan.plain_es: Es el préstamo hipotecario a 30 años más grande que podría pagar un hogar con el ingreso mediano del municipio. Se aplican tres supuestos. La vivienda consume 30% del ingreso. Cerca del 78% de ese presupuesto (23.5% del ingreso) paga el préstamo. La tasa de interés es fija de 5%. Es una referencia, no el límite de un prestamista.
municipalities.max_affordable_loan.definition: A calculation on the median household income of the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. Housing may take 30% of income. 78% of that housing budget goes to principal and interest, the part of a mortgage payment that repays the loan and pays the lender (the study's own proportion: $430 of $549). The result is the loan that this monthly payment repays over 30 years at a fixed 5% yearly interest rate. The loan is in the same dollars as the income: the dollars of the window's last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). It follows the method of Table 6 (Table 8 in the study PDF) of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, published by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) in 2023.
municipalities.max_affordable_loan.method: monthly housing budget = median household income × 0.30 ÷ 12. Monthly principal and interest = budget × 430/549 (about 0.7832). With r = 0.05 ÷ 12, loan = payment × (1 − (1 + r)^−360) ÷ r, rounded to a whole dollar. In short, the loan is about 3.65 times median household income. The rate (5%) and the principal-and-interest share (430/549) are fixed settings of the observatory's build. The 30% income share and the 360-month term are written into the calculation itself.
municipalities.max_affordable_loan.how_to_read: A higher amount means a typical household in the municipality could borrow more under these assumptions. Compare it with the median home value through the affordability ratio. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write: 'Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory; calculated from US Census Bureau ACS 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B19013, with the affordability method of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023).'
caveats: The 30% share, the 78% share (430 of 549) and the 30-year term follow the study's Table 6 method. The 5% rate is the one the study states in its endnotes for the maximum mortgage (a bank's mortgage calculator, assuming no other debt, homeowners' association fees or taxes). The study's published maximums imply 4.994%, so the observatory's figures at exactly 5% run $19 to $65 below them. None of these is a lender's rule. Real rates and lending rules differ.
The calculation leaves out the down payment, closing costs, credit history and any other debt.
It uses the median income of all households, renters and owners alike, not of people who plan to buy.
The method gives $80,127 for the study's Puerto Rico median income of $21,967. The study prints $80,181, a gap of $54.
No margin of error is calculated for this field. It inherits the survey margin of the income it is based on.
An illustration of one set of assumptions across municipalities. It is not financial or lending advice and not an estimate of what any household can borrow.

municipalities.gross_rent_change_pct.plain: How much the median monthly rent changed between the 2008-2012 survey window and the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), in percent. Each window is in the dollars of its own last year (2012 and 2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), so general price rises are still in the number.
municipalities.gross_rent_change_pct.plain_es: Cuánto cambió el alquiler mensual mediano entre la ventana de encuesta 2008-2012 y la más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10), en por ciento. Cada ventana está en dólares de su propio último año (2012 y 2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10), así que el alza general de precios sigue incluida en el número.
municipalities.gross_rent_change_pct.definition: (median_gross_rent in the latest window minus median_gross_rent in the 2008-2012 window) divided by the 2008-2012 value, times 100. The latest window is 2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot. Both medians are table B25064 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. The Census Bureau reports ACS dollar amounts in the dollars of the last year of each window, so the 2008-2012 window is in 2012 dollars and the latest window is in the dollars of its last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The observatory makes no conversion between windows.
municipalities.gross_rent_change_pct.method: Calculated as round((new − old) ÷ old × 100, 1), where new is B25064 cell 001 for the latest window and old is the same cell for 2008-2012. The field is empty if the old value is missing or zero.
municipalities.gross_rent_change_pct.how_to_read: A positive value means current renters pay more per month than renters did in 2008-2012, in unadjusted dollars. A value near the general rise in prices over the same years means rents kept pace with prices. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 54 of 78 municipalities show a change smaller than the 36.6% rise in the US CPI-U over 2012 to 2024, and 2 of them show a fall in dollars. On the Housing page you can choose another base year, and the page then shows a different comparison. This field always compares 2008-2012 with the latest window. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012, table B25064, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory'.
caveats: The observatory does not convert 2012 dollars to 2024 dollars, so the change includes general price rises. For scale, the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) rose 36.6% from 2012 to 2024 (annual averages, stored in economy_series.json). The CPI-U is a US index of all consumer prices. It is not a Puerto Rico index and not a measure of rent or home-price inflation, so it is only a rough scale.

Both ends are survey estimates with their own margins of error. A small change in a small municipality can be noise. The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, the largest increase, in Villalba (+85.3%), rests on medians with margins of error of ±$59 in 2008-2012 and ±$133 in 2020-2024.

housing.owner_cost_burden_pct.plain: Out of every 100 owner households with a mortgage, how many spend 30% or more of their income on owner costs: mortgage, taxes, insurance and utilities. Puerto Rico: 36.4% in the 2020-2024 window. Owners without a mortgage are not counted.
housing.owner_cost_burden_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares propietarios con hipoteca, cuántos gastan 30% o más de su ingreso en costos de propiedad: hipoteca, contribuciones, seguros y servicios. Puerto Rico: 36.4% en la ventana 2020-2024. Los propietarios sin hipoteca no se cuentan.
housing.owner_cost_burden_pct.definition: Owner households with a mortgage whose selected monthly owner costs are 30% or more of household income (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25091, cells 8 to 11) divided by owner households with a mortgage whose ratio can be computed (cell 2 minus cell 12, 'Not computed'), times 100. Selected monthly owner costs add the monthly payments for mortgages and similar debts, property taxes, property insurance, utilities and fuel, plus condominium or mobile-home fees where they apply. They do not include repairs or maintenance.
housing.owner_cost_burden_pct.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 8, 9, 10 and 11 and divides by cell 2 minus cell 12. The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator. The same arithmetic over bands 3 to 11 gives the island-wide distribution in the study's Table 4.
housing.owner_cost_burden_pct.how_to_read: A value of 36 means that about 36 of every 100 owners with a mortgage spend 30% or more of income on owner costs. The costs include utilities and taxes, so the share is higher than a mortgage payment alone would give. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Owners with no mortgage are outside the base, although they can also be burdened by taxes, insurance and repairs.

Very noisy in small municipalities. Culebra shows 61.5% in 2020-2024 with a margin of ± 46.3 points; Vieques shows 0.0% in the 2015-2019 and 2016-2020 windows, with about 76 owner households with a mortgage in the first of them (margin ± 73 households). The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.
In Puerto Rico in 2020-2024, 4,803 of 324,311 owner households with a mortgage (1.5%) are in the 'Not computed' group and are left out of the base.

The page also prints 36.5% for 2020-2024 beside the Table 4 chart, because it adds the four rounded bands (7.4 + 5.8 + 6.8 + 16.5). This series divides unrounded counts and gives 36.43, which shows as 36.4%. The two can differ by 0.1 point.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.

municipalities.owner_cost_burden_pct.plain_es: La proporción de hogares propietarios con hipoteca que pagan 30% o más de su ingreso en costos de vivienda. Se excluyen los propietarios sin hipoteca. En el corte de datos de 2026-10 son cerca de 6 de cada 10 hogares propietarios en los 78 municipios.
municipalities.owner_cost_burden_pct.definition: Owner households with a mortgage whose selected monthly owner costs are 30% or more of household income, divided by owner households with a mortgage for which that share can be computed, times 100. From table B25091 (mortgage status by selected monthly owner costs as a percentage of household income) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). Selected monthly owner costs include the mortgage payment, property taxes, insurance, utilities and fuel.
municipalities.owner_cost_burden_pct.method: B25091 cells 008 to 011 added, divided by (cell 002 'Housing units with a mortgage' minus cell 012 'Not computed'), times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b25091.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).
municipalities.owner_cost_burden_pct.how_to_read: A high value means many owners who are still paying a mortgage spend a large part of their income on housing. It says nothing about owners without a mortgage.
caveats: Owners without a mortgage are not counted. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window) they are about 63% of owner households across the 78 municipalities (552,275 of 876,586).
Owners whose ratio cannot be computed are also left out (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 4,803 of 324,311 owner households with a mortgage).

Small groups make the estimate unstable. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±2.1 points (San Juan) to ±46.3 points (Culebra). housing.renter_cost_burden_pct.plain: Out of every 100 renter households for which the Census Bureau could compute it, how many pay 30% or more of their income in rent. Puerto Rico: 50.8% in the 2020-2024 window. Households that pay no cash rent or have no income are not in the count.
housing.renter_cost_burden_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares inquilinos para los que el Negociado del Censo pudo calcularlo, cuántos pagan 30% o más de su ingreso en alquiler. Puerto Rico: 50.8% en la ventana 2020-2024. Los hogares que no pagan alquiler en efectivo o que no tienen ingresos no entran en el conteo.
housing.renter_cost_burden_pct.definition: Renter households paying 30% or more of household income in gross rent (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25070, cells 7 to 10) divided by renter households whose ratio can be computed (cell 1 minus cell 11, 'Not computed'), times 100. Gross rent includes utilities and fuels paid by the renter. The bands start at 30.0%, so a household paying exactly 30% is counted.
housing.renter_cost_burden_pct.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 7, 8, 9 and 10 and divides by cell 1 minus cell 11. The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator. The same arithmetic summed over bands 2 to 10 gives the island-wide distribution in the study's Table 3.
housing.renter_cost_burden_pct.how_to_read: A value of 50 means that half of the renter households in the base spend 30% or more of income on rent. The 30% line is the common rule of thumb for cost burden, not a measure of hardship. It does not say how much money is left after rent. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: In Puerto Rico in 2020-2024, 173,394 of 414,280 renter households (42%) are in the Census Bureau's 'Not computed' group, which includes households that pay no cash rent and households with no or negative income. They are left out of the base, so the percentage describes the other 58%.

Noisy in small municipalities: in the 2026-10 snapshot, 736 of 1,170 municipality estimates have a margin of error larger than 30% of the estimate. Culebra in 2020-2024 shows 22.0% with a margin of ± 24.2 points. The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.

housing.median_rent_pct_income.plain: The middle share of income that renter households spend on rent. Half spend a larger share, half a smaller one. Puerto Rico: 30.4% in the 2020-2024 window.

housing.median_rent_pct_income.definition: Median, across renter households for which it can be computed, of gross rent divided by household income (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25071, cell 1). Gross rent includes utilities and fuels paid by the renter.
housing.median_rent_pct_income.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. housing.median_rent_pct_income.how_to_read: A value of 30 means half of renter households pay 30% or more of their income in rent. It is the middle of the households' own ratios. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Households for which the Census Bureau cannot compute the ratio, such as those paying no cash rent or with no or negative income, are left out. The data hold no count of that group for this table. For scale, the 'Not computed' group in table B25070 (a different table, used for the cost-burden shares) is 173,394 of 414,280 renter households in Puerto Rico (42%) in 2020-2024.

Noisy in small municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 153 of the 1,165 municipality estimates that have a margin of error (1,170 in all) have a margin larger than 30% of the estimate. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, five municipality estimates have no margin of error: Barranquitas, Florida and Las Marías in 2013-2017 (50.0), Barranquitas in 2014-2018 (51.0) and Naranjito in 2018-2022 (51.0). In the 2013-2017 and 2014-2018 files the margin field holds a dot (no value); in the 2018-2022 file it is the code -333333333, which the Census Bureau uses when a median falls in an open-ended interval (here, 50% or more of income). Read these values as '50% or more'.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 64% of barrios and 66% of census tracts that have a value. A median at the edge of an open-ended interval (the Census Bureau prints the boundary) or equal to 0 is not an estimate and is left empty (47 barrios and 74 census tracts in 2020-2024). See methods.small_area_estimates.

credit.hmda_loan_amount.plain: How much money in home loans lenders made in each municipio during the year.
credit.hmda_loan_amount.plain_es: Cuánto dinero en préstamos hipotecarios otorgaron los prestamistas en cada municipio durante el año.
credit.hmda_loan_amount.definition: The sum of the home loans made in the municipio during the year, in dollars of each year. The public file gives each loan as the midpoint of its $10,000 band, so the sum is within $5,000 a loan of the true amount. A municipio with fewer than 10 loans in a year has no value: the observatory does not publish a figure that could describe a few borrowers.
credit.hmda_loan_amount.method: credit.py reads the public HMDA file for Puerto Rico, one row for each application a reporting lender received, 2018-2025, and adds the rows up by the municipio of the home (county_code). Loans bought from another lender (action 6) are left out. A loan made is action 1; a decided application is action 1, 2 (approved, not taken) or 3 (denied). Rows with no municipio count in Puerto Rico's figure only (62 in 2025). The rows describe single borrowers, so nothing below the municipio is published and a municipio-year with fewer than 10 loans or decided applications has no amount or denial share.
credit.hmda_loan_amount.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: $2.86 billion in 2025 ($1.69 billion in 2018). Most: San Juan ($476.3 million), Bayamón ($229.1 million), Carolina ($174.7 million). The Data Browser's own total for 2023 is the same: 13,550 loans and $2.24 billion.
caveats: Dollars of each year, not adjusted for inflation.
Each loan is the midpoint of its $10,000 band in the public file, so a sum is within $5,000 a loan of the true amount.
Lenders below HMDA's reporting thresholds are missing, so the counts are less than all home lending.
credit.hmda_loan_amount.source_detail: Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data, Puerto Rico, 2018-2025 (FFIEC and CFPB Data Browser)

credit.hmda_denial_pct.plain: Out of every 100 home loan applications lenders decided in a municipio, how many they denied.
credit.hmda_denial_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 solicitudes de préstamo hipotecario que los prestamistas decidieron en un municipio, cuántas denegaron.
credit.hmda_denial_pct.definition: Of the applications for a home loan in the municipio that a lender decided during the year (made, approved but not taken, or denied), the share denied. Applications withdrawn or closed as incomplete are left out. A denial depends on the applicant's income, debts and credit and on the home, which this share does not separate. A municipio with fewer than 10 decided applications in a year has no value: the observatory does not publish a figure that could describe a few borrowers.
credit.hmda_denial_pct.method: credit.py reads the public HMDA file for Puerto Rico, one row for each application a reporting lender received, 2018-2025, and adds the rows up by the municipio of the home (county_code). Loans bought from another lender (action 6) are left out. A loan made is action 1; a decided application is action 1, 2 (approved, not taken) or 3 (denied). Rows with no municipio count in Puerto Rico's figure only (62 in 2025). The rows describe single borrowers, so nothing below the municipio is published and a municipio-year with fewer than 10 loans or decided applications has no amount or denial share.
credit.hmda_denial_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 18.5% in 2025 (26.2% in 2018). Highest: Guánica (39.5%), Maunabo (35.5%), Villalba (31.2%). A municipio with few applications moves a lot: read the count of loans beside it.
caveats: A denial depends on the applicant's income, debts and credit and on the home; the share does not separate them and says nothing about why.
Applications withdrawn or closed as incomplete are not counted as denied.
Lenders below HMDA's reporting thresholds are missing, so the counts are less than all home lending.

municipalities.housing_units_2010.plain: How many homes the 2010 Census counted in the municipality on April 1, 2010, whether or not people lived in them.
municipalities.housing_units_2010.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda contó el Censo de 2010 en el municipio el 1 de abril de 2010, estuvieran ocupadas o no.
municipalities.housing_units_2010.definition: The 2010 Census count of housing units (field HU100) of the municipality, occupied or vacant. The 78 values add up to 1,636,946 units.
municipalities.housing_units_2010.method: Read from the HU100 field of TIGERweb (the Census Bureau's online map and data service) 2010 layer 100 and matched to the 2020 municipalities by the five-digit municipality code (GEOID, the Census Bureau's geographic identifier). The observatory does not calculate a change from it; it is stored beside the 2020 count.
municipalities.housing_units_2010.how_to_read: In the 2010 Census, San Juan had the most housing units (199,915) and Culebra the fewest (1,603). Subtract it from housing_units_2020 for the change in homes. Between the 2010 and 2020 Censuses, 15 municipalities gained housing units and 63 lost them; the island total fell by 2.4% (1,636,946 to 1,598,159). Maricao lost the largest share (15.3%) and Aibonito gained the largest (5.2%); both shares and the 2.4% are worked out from the municipal values, not stored in the file.
caveats: A fall in units can come from demolition, storm damage or a change in how the census counted addresses; the field does not say which.
The map does not display this field; it is in the data file and in the CSV (comma-separated values) download.
municipalities.housing_units_2010.source_detail: Census TIGERweb 2010 counties layer 100, STATE = '72', field HU100; downloaded 2026-10-01. The 78 values equal the 2010 Census counts of Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) table H1 held in the entry 'Housing units, census count (number)'.

municipalities.housing_units_2020.plain: How many homes the 2020 Census counted in the municipality on April 1, 2020, whether or not people lived in them.
municipalities.housing_units_2020.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda contó el Censo de 2020 en el municipio el 1 de abril de 2020, estuvieran ocupadas o no.
municipalities.housing_units_2020.definition: The 2020 Census count of housing units (field HU100) of the municipality, occupied or vacant. The Census Bureau defines a housing unit as a house, apartment, mobile home, group of rooms or single room meant as separate living quarters. The 78 values add up to 1,598,159 units.
municipalities.housing_units_2020.method: Read from the HU100 field of TIGERweb (the Census Bureau's online map and data service) layer 82 and stored without change. housing.py divides population_2020 by this count to get residents per housing unit.
municipalities.housing_units_2020.how_to_read: In the 2020 Census, San Juan has the most housing units (193,244) and Culebra the fewest (1,563). It counts all homes, including vacant and seasonal ones, so it is larger than the number of households.
caveats: It is a census count, not a sample estimate. The American Community Survey's housing_units (see 'Housing units (number)') is an estimate with a margin of error and will not match it.

municipalities.affordability_method.plain: The observatory uses the affordability method of the 2023 housing study by Foundation for Puerto Rico (Table 6 on the Housing page and in this dictionary; Table 8 in the study PDF). It turns median income into the largest 30-year loan a household could carry, then compares that loan with the median home value. This entry lists the settings. In the list below, the 'Code' column holds the method's settings, not coded values.
municipalities.affordability_method.plain_es: El observatorio usa el método de asequibilidad del estudio de vivienda de 2023 de Foundation for Puerto Rico (Tabla 6 en la página "Vivienda" y en este diccionario; Tabla 8 en el PDF del estudio). Convierte el ingreso mediano en el préstamo a 30 años más grande que podría pagar un hogar y luego compara ese préstamo con el valor mediano de la vivienda. Esta ficha presenta los parámetros. En la lista de abajo, la columna "Código" contiene los parámetros del método, no valores codificados.
municipalities.affordability_method.definition: A four-step calculation. The method comes from The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, published by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) in 2023 (Table 6 here; Table 8 in the study PDF). (1) Take the median household income of the window (table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates). (2) A household may spend 30% of its income on housing, so the monthly housing budget is income × 0.30 ÷ 12. (3) Of that budget, 430/549 (about 78.3%) goes to principal and interest, the part of the payment that repays the loan and pays the lender. (4) The maximum loan is the amount that this payment repays in full over 360 monthly payments at a fixed 5% yearly rate. The affordability ratio is median home value divided by that loan.
municipalities.affordability_method.method: With r = 0.05 ÷ 12: loan = income × 0.30 ÷ 12 × (430/549) × (1 − (1 + r)^−360) ÷ r, rounded to a whole dollar. Multiplier: about 3.6476 × income. Ratio = median_home_value ÷ loan, rounded to two decimals. The Housing page series uses the same formula for every year. Check against the study: income $21,967 gives $80,127; the study prints $80,181 for Puerto Rico (a gap of $54).
municipalities.affordability_method.how_to_read: Use the ratio to compare municipalities with each other under one set of assumptions. Do not use it to say whether a particular family can buy a particular home. Worked example from the 2026-10 snapshot (Guaynabo, 2020-2024 window): median household income $46,731 gives a housing budget of about $1,168 a month, about $915 of it for principal and interest, and a maximum loan of $170,456. The median home value is $226,800, so the ratio is 1.33.
caveats: The 30% share, the 78% share ($430 of $549) and the 30-year term are the study's. The 5% rate is the one the study states in its endnotes for the maximum mortgage (a bank's mortgage calculator, assuming no other debt, homeowners' association fees or taxes). The study's published maximums imply 4.994%, so the observatory's figures at exactly 5% run $19 to $65 below them. The Housing page notes that actual mortgage rates ranged from under 4% to over 7% over the period it covers.
The method has no down payment, closing costs, credit score or other debt.

Table numbers: this dictionary and the Housing page call the study's affordability table Table 6. The study PDF prints it as Table 8. See 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023): figures and tables on the Housing page'.
Calculated by the observatory from public Census Bureau data. The Census Bureau does not publish it, and no margin of error is calculated for it.

values.30%: Share of income that housing may take.
values.430/549: Share of the housing budget that goes to principal and interest (about 78.3%), the study's own proportion ($430 of $549).
values.5%: Fixed yearly interest rate, the one the study states. Held at 5% in every window and municipality.
values.ratio above 1.00: After rounding to two decimals, the median home costs more than the maximum loan: 'out of reach' in the Housing page profile, a warning color on the map's Municipality tab.
values.ratio of 1.00 or less: After rounding to two decimals, the median home costs no more than the maximum loan: 'within reach' in the Housing page profile, green on the map's Municipality tab. Because the test uses the rounded ratio, a home that costs slightly more than the maximum loan can still show 1.00 and count as 'within reach'. In the 2026-10 snapshot this is the case for Guayanilla: its median home ($87,400) is $168 above its maximum loan ($87,232), and the ratio rounds to 1.00.

municipalities.affordability_method.source_detail: FPR (2023), The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, Table 6 (Table 8 in the study PDF); ACS 5-year tables B19013 and B25077

municipalities.change_method.plain: Each change field compares the latest five-year survey window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot) with the 2008-2012 window for the same municipality. Dollar changes are not adjusted for inflation. In the list below, the 'Code' column holds field names, not coded values.
municipalities.change_method.plain_es: Cada campo de cambio compara la ventana de encuesta de cinco años más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10) con la ventana 2008-2012 del mismo municipio. Los cambios en dólares no se ajustan por inflación. En la lista de abajo, la columna "Código" contiene nombres de campos, no valores codificados.
municipalities.change_method.definition: Percent changes are (latest minus baseline) divided by baseline, times 100, rounded to one decimal. The education change is the latest share minus the baseline share, in percentage points. The two windows share no survey years. The baseline is the 2008-2012 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year release, a fixed comparison window of the observatory, read from the Census Bureau's Puerto Rico sequence files. The latest window is read from the table-based summary files (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
municipalities.change_method.method: The observatory reads the two windows separately and calculates each change from the two medians or shares. The comparison is nominal: the observatory makes no conversion between windows. The Census Bureau reports each window's dollars in its last year (2012 for the baseline; 2024 for the latest window in the 2026-10 snapshot). The 2008-2012 income table is titled 'in 2012 inflation-adjusted dollars'; the 2012 titles for home value and rent say only '(DOLLARS)'. The Housing page computes the same kind of change for a base year you choose and says it is not adjusted for inflation.
municipalities.change_method.how_to_read: Read a change as 'higher or lower than in 2008-2012', not as a measured yearly trend. Remember that prices in general rose between the two windows.
caveats: The observatory does not convert 2012 dollars to 2024 dollars, so the change includes general price rises. For scale, the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) rose 36.6% from 2012 to 2024 (annual averages, stored in economy_series.json). The CPI-U is a US index of all consumer prices. It is not a Puerto Rico index and not a measure of rent or home-price inflation, so it is only a rough scale.
Only two points in time are compared. What happened between them, such as hurricanes and population loss, is not shown by these fields; the Housing page series has every window.
No margin of error is calculated for a change. Both ends are survey estimates.

housing.homeowner_vacancy_pct.plain: Out of every 100 owner homes, how many are empty and for sale. Owner homes are those lived in by their owners, for sale, or sold but not yet occupied. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.homeowner_vacancy_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 viviendas de propietarios, cuántas están desocupadas y en venta. Las viviendas de propietarios son las que ocupan sus dueños, las que están en venta y las vendidas que aún no se han ocupado. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.homeowner_vacancy_pct.definition: Units for sale only divided by all owner units, times 100. Owner units are units for sale only, units sold but not yet occupied, and owner-occupied units. From American Community Survey (ACS) tables B25004 and B25003.
housing.homeowner_vacancy_pct.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25004 cell 004 (for sale only) / [B25004 cell 004 + B25004 cell 005 (sold, not occupied) + B25003 cell 002 (owner-occupied)] x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 1.3% with a margin of ±0.1 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. The margins of the three cells that make up the denominator are first combined the same way, by taking the square root of the sum of their squares. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
housing.homeowner_vacancy_pct.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide rate is 2.44% in 2006-2010, peaks at 3.74% in 2011-2015 and is 1.30% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.09 percentage points). In 2020-2024 the highest value is Sabana Grande (6.40%). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: Small base, wide swings. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 66 of the 78 municipalities have a margin of error above 30% of a non-zero estimate in the 2020-2024 window (only the Housing page's full-data table shows these in italics). The page does not italicize the ten municipalities with an estimate of zero (see the next caution). Treat small differences between municipalities as noise.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 10 municipalities have an estimate of zero in the 2020-2024 window. It means the survey found no homes for sale in its sample, not that none exist. Each zero carries a margin of error (0.32 to 1.05 percentage points).
It leaves out vacant homes that are not for sale, such as seasonal and 'other vacant' homes, so it is far lower than overall vacancy.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

Each window pools five years of interviews, so it does not describe conditions on one date. The windows labeled 2017 to 2021 include the 2017 hurricane season, and those labeled 2020 to 2024 include the pandemic years. The data alone cannot show why a figure changed.

municipalities.housing_units_acs.plain: The number of homes in the municipality, occupied or empty, as the Census Bureau's five-year survey estimates it. It is a survey estimate, not the 2020 census count.
municipalities.housing_units_acs.plain_es: El número de viviendas en el municipio, ocupadas o desocupadas, según el estimado de la encuesta de cinco años del Negociado del Censo. Es un estimado de encuesta, no el conteo del Censo de 2020.
municipalities.housing_units_acs.definition: All housing units, occupied and vacant, from table B25002 (occupancy status), cell 001 ('Total'), of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). municipalities.housing_units_acs.method: Copied unchanged from ACS table B25002, cell 001 (file acsdt5y2024-b25002.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot). It is the denominator of vacancy_pct and seasonal_pct. The Housing page series reads the same count from table B25001. In the 2026-10 snapshot the two agree for all 78 municipalities.
municipalities.housing_units_acs.how_to_read: Use it as the base for the vacancy and seasonal shares in the same window. For the count taken on census day 2020, use 'Housing units, 2020 Census'. This is a count, so it is largest where the municipality is largest. To compare municipalities of different size, use a share, such as 'Vacant housing units (%)'.
caveats: It differs from the 2020 census count ('Housing units, 2020 Census'). In the 2026-10 snapshot, across the 78 municipalities, the survey figure is between 97% and 112% of the census figure.

housing.census_housing_units.plain: How many homes the census counted in each municipality on April 1, 2010 and April 1, 2020. A home counts whether or not people live in it.
housing.census_housing_units.plain_es: Cuántas viviendas contó el Censo en cada municipio el 1 de abril de 2010 y el 1 de abril de 2020. Una vivienda cuenta tanto si vive gente en ella como si no.
housing.census_housing_units.definition: All housing units counted on census day, from table H1 of the Census Bureau's Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) redistricting data. A housing unit is a house, apartment, mobile home or room meant as separate living quarters. It counts whether or not anyone lives there. Dormitories, nursing homes and other group housing are not housing units.
housing.census_housing_units.method: Read from the Census Bureau's Puerto Rico Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) redistricting files (pr2010.pl.zip and pr2020.pl.zip), table H1 (housing occupancy). H1 holds three numbers per area: total housing units, occupied and vacant. Municipality rows are summary level 050 and the island row is level 040. This variable is the total.
housing.census_housing_units.how_to_read: These are census counts, not a survey sample, so there is no sampling margin of error. The Census Bureau holds the total number of housing units exact in 2020 (it adds no privacy noise to this total). Island-wide: 1,636,946 units in 2010 and 1,598,159 in 2020, a fall of 2.4%. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the same counts appear in municipalities.json as housing_units_2010 and housing_units_2020 (read from the Census Bureau's TIGERweb layers) and match for all 78 municipalities, and the island count equals the sum of the 78 municipality counts in both years.
caveats: Only two years exist (2010 and 2020). Nothing is published for the years between.

The American Community Survey (ACS) also estimates housing units (housing.housing_units), and its totals differ. The 2006-2010 window is 162,920 units below the 2010 census count (1,474,026 against 1,636,946). The 2016-2020 window is 38,183 below the 2020 count (1,559,976 against 1,598,159). Use one source at a time.
The count does not say how many of the homes are fit to live in.

housing.housing_units.definition: All housing units, occupied or vacant, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25001. A housing unit is a house, apartment, mobile home or room meant as separate living quarters.
housing.housing_units.method: ACS 5-year table B25001 (Housing Units), cell 001, taken as the Census Bureau publishes it. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The file carries the Census Bureau's margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) for each municipality and window, in housing units.
housing.housing_units.how_to_read: Use it for the size of the housing stock and as the base of the vacancy shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide count is 1,474,026 in 2006-2010 and 1,634,357 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 4,364). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error. caveats: ACS totals differ from the census counts. The 2006-2010 window is 162,920 units below the 2010 census count, and the 2016-2020 window is 38,183 below the 2020 count (see housing.census_housing_units). Use one source at a time.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2020-2024 window is 59,252 units (3.8%) above the 2019-2023 window. Earlier steps between windows ran from -0.4% to +1.9%. The household count also steps up between the same two windows (+4.2%; see housing.households). The observatory shows the figure as the Census Bureau published it. The data do not explain the jump, so do not read the step as new construction.
It is a survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, none of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of its estimate in the 2020-2024 window.

housing.median_year_built.plain_es: El año del medio en que se construyeron las viviendas del municipio: la mitad se construyó antes de ese año y la mitad después. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.median_year_built.definition: Median year the structure was built, for all housing units, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25035. The value is a calendar year, such as 1979.
housing.median_year_built.method: ACS 5-year table B25035 (Median Year Structure Built), cell 001, taken as the Census Bureau publishes it. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The file carries the Census Bureau's margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) for each municipality and window, in years.
housing.median_year_built.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide median is 1976 in 2006-2010 and 1979 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 1 year). In 2020-2024 it runs from 1967 (San Juan) to 1996 (Culebra). An older year means an older housing stock. The median moves slowly: new homes and demolitions shift it by only a few years between the windows labeled 2010 and 2024. Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: It describes the year of construction, not the condition of the home. An old home can be well kept, and a newer home can be damaged.
The year comes from survey answers, not from building records, and it covers occupied and vacant homes together.
It is a survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, none of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of its estimate in the 2020-2024 window.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

housing.mobile_home_pct.plain: Out of every 100 homes, how many are mobile homes. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.mobile_home_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 viviendas, cuántas son casas móviles. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.mobile_home_pct.definition: Housing units that are mobile homes divided by all housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25024.
housing.mobile_home_pct.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25024 cell 010 (mobile home) / B25024 cell 001 (all housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 0.2%). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
housing.mobile_home_pct.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, mobile homes are rare in Puerto Rico: 0.21% of housing units in 2006-2010 and 0.22% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.02 percentage points). In 2020-2024 the highest share is Cabo Rojo (2.21%). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.

Boats, recreational vehicles and vans (a separate category in the table) are not included.

housing.other_vacant_units.plain_es: El número estimado de viviendas desocupadas que no están en alquiler, en venta ni son de temporada. Es la medida pública que suele usarse para aproximar la vivienda abandonada, pero no es un conteo de viviendas abandonadas. housing.other_vacant_units.definition: Vacant housing units whose reason for being vacant is none of the named reasons, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25004 (Vacancy Status), the 'other vacant' category.
housing.other_vacant_units.method: ACS 5-year table B25004 (Vacancy Status), cell 008 (Other vacant), taken as the Census Bureau publishes it. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The file carries the Census Bureau's margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) for each municipality and window, in housing units.
housing.other_vacant_units.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide count is 128,526 in 2006-2010 and 222,697 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 3,086), which is 64.8% of all vacant units in 2020-2024 against 52.0% in 2006-2010. Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error. In the same snapshot, the Puerto Rico count equals the sum of the 78 municipality counts in every window.
caveats: 'Other vacant' is the Census Bureau's catch-all: a vacant unit that fits none of the named reasons (for rent, rented not yet occupied, for sale, sold not yet occupied, seasonal or occasional use, for migrant workers). The Census Bureau's definitions sort it further into reasons such as foreclosure, personal or family reasons, legal proceedings including an estate, needs repairs, being repaired, extended absence, and abandoned or possibly condemned (ACS 2024 Subject Definitions, 'Other Vacancy Status'). The observatory's data do not separate these, so it is not a count of abandoned homes.
The Housing page also quotes the 2023 Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) study's estimate of 300,000 dilapidated or abandoned units. That is the study's estimate, not this variable.

housing.overcrowded_pct.plain: Out of every 100 homes where people live, how many have more than one person for every room. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 2.3% with a margin of ±0.1 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. The margins of the cells in the numerator are first combined by taking the square root of the sum of their squares. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
housing.overcrowded_pct.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide share falls from 5.79% in 2006-2010 to 2.26% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.12 percentage points). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: The share is of occupied homes only. Empty homes are not in the denominator.

housing.residents_per_unit.plain: On average, how many residents there are for each home, lived in or empty, on census day in 2010 and 2020. A lower number means more homes for each resident.

housing.residents_per_unit.definition: Population divided by census housing units in the same year (2010 or 2020).
housing.residents_per_unit.method: Computed in housing_series.py as population / census housing units, rounded to two decimals. Population is housing.population for 2010 and 2020 (in the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2020 value is the April 1, 2020 base of the Vintage 2025 estimates, the 2025 release of the Census Bureau's yearly estimates, built on the 2020 census). Housing units are the table H1 total (housing.census_housing_units).
housing.residents_per_unit.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide ratio falls from 2.28 in 2010 to 2.06 in 2020, because the population fell 11.8% while housing units fell 2.4%. Culebra has the lowest ratio (1.13 in 2010, 1.15 in 2020). The 2020 values equal municipalities.json:residents_per_unit.
caveats: This is not household size. It divides by every housing unit, including empty ones, and counts every resident, including people in group housing. Average household size (housing.avg_household_size) divides by occupied homes only.
A low ratio can come from many empty or seasonal homes, as in Culebra, and not only from small households.

The population in this ratio comes from the Census Bureau's Population Estimates files (CENSUS2010POP and the April 1, 2020 base), not from table P1 of the redistricting data. It is a ratio of two census-based figures and has no margin of error.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

municipalities.seasonal_units.plain: The number of empty homes kept for seasonal, recreational or occasional use, such as weekend and vacation homes. It is the nearest public count of weekend homes.
municipalities.seasonal_units.plain_es: El número de viviendas desocupadas que se reservan para uso de temporada, recreativo u ocasional, como las casas de fin de semana y de vacaciones. Es el conteo público que más se acerca al número de casas de fin de semana.
municipalities.seasonal_units.definition: Vacant housing units whose vacancy status is 'For seasonal, recreational, or occasional use': table B25004, cell 006, of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
municipalities.seasonal_units.method: Copied unchanged from ACS table B25004, cell 006 (file acsdt5y2024-b25004.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).
municipalities.seasonal_units.how_to_read: Use it as an indirect sign of weekend and second homes. The Housing page treats it as the closest public stand-in for weekend homes and short-term rentals, but the Census Bureau has no short-term rental category, so this is not a count of short-term rentals. This is a count, so it is largest where the municipality is largest. To compare municipalities, use 'Seasonal, recreational or occasional-use units (%)'.
caveats: The Census Bureau has no separate category for short-term rentals, so they are not identified in this count. It is an indirect measure only.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±50 (Florida) to ±649 (San Juan). In the same snapshot, Florida's margin (±50) is larger than its estimate (30).

housing.seasonal_pct.plain: Out of every 100 homes, how many are empty and kept for vacations, weekends or other occasional use, estimated from a 5-year survey. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.seasonal_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 viviendas, cuántas están desocupadas y se reservan para vacaciones, fines de semana u otro uso ocasional, según el estimado de una encuesta de 5 años. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.seasonal_pct.definition: Vacant housing units held for seasonal, recreational or occasional use divided by all housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) tables B25004 and B25001.
housing.seasonal_pct.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25004 cell 006 (seasonal, recreational or occasional use) / B25001 cell 001 (all housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 4.6% with a margin of ±0.1 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
housing.seasonal_pct.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide share is 3.92% in 2006-2010 and 4.61% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.10 percentage points). In 2020-2024 Culebra has 40.74% and Vieques 24.13%; the lowest is Sabana Grande (0.54%). The Housing page describes it as the closest public stand-in (a proxy) for weekend homes and short-term rentals; the first caution below gives the limit. Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: The Census Bureau's vacancy categories (table B25004; see the ACS 2024 Subject Definitions, 'Vacancy Status') have no short-term rental class, so a home rented to visitors has no category of its own here. Do not read this variable as a short-term rental count.

The share is a share of all housing units, not of vacant units, and the home must be vacant at the time of the survey to be counted. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 39 of the 78 municipalities have a margin of error above 30% of the estimate in the 2020-2024 window (only the Housing page's full-data table shows these in italics). Treat small differences between municipalities as noise.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 97% of barrios and 97% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.

If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
housing.detached_house_pct.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide share is 67.90% in 2006-2010 and 68.03% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.24 percentage points), so the mix has barely moved. housing.apartments_5plus_pct.plain: Out of every 100 homes, how many are in a building with five or more homes. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.apartments_5plus_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 viviendas, cuántas están en un edificio de cinco viviendas o más. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.apartments_5plus_pct.definition: Housing units in structures with five or more units divided by all housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25024.
housing.apartments_5plus_pct.method: Computed in housing_series.py: [B25024 cell 006 (5 to 9 units) + cell 007 (10 to 19) + cell 008 (20 to 49) + cell 009 (50 or more)] / B25024 cell 001 (all housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 13.9% with a margin of ±0.2 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. The margins of the cells in the numerator are first combined by taking the square root of the sum of their squares. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
housing.apartments_5plus_pct.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide share is 12.76% in 2006-2010 and 13.93% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.22 percentage points). In 2020-2024 it runs from 0.86% (Peñuelas) to 41.42% (San Juan). A high share means more of the homes, occupied or empty, are in buildings with five or more units. It does not give the share of people who live in them. Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: Buildings with two to four units are not in this share, so it does not equal 'all apartments'.

housing.census_vacancy_pct.plain: Out of every 100 homes, how many were empty on census day (April 1) in 2010 and 2020.
housing.census_vacancy_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 viviendas, cuántas estaban desocupadas el día del Censo (1 de abril) en 2010 y 2020.
housing.census_vacancy_pct.definition: Vacant housing units divided by all housing units on census day, times 100.
housing.census_vacancy_pct.method: Read from the Census Bureau's Puerto Rico Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) redistricting files (pr2010.pl.zip and pr2020.pl.zip), table H1 (housing occupancy). H1 holds three numbers per area: total housing units, occupied and vacant. Municipality rows are summary level 050 and the island row is level 040. This variable is the vacant count divided by the total, times 100, rounded to two decimals (computed in housing_series.py). The data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example 16.1% for Puerto Rico in 2020).
housing.census_vacancy_pct.how_to_read: Island-wide the rate is 15.91% in 2010 and 16.12% in 2020. In 2020 it runs from 8.00% (Aibonito) to 50.16% (Culebra). It comes from census counts, not a survey, so it has no sampling margin of error (for 2020, see the privacy-noise caution).
caveats: The American Community Survey (ACS) gives a higher vacancy rate (housing.vacancy_pct). For 2016-2020 it is 22.71% against 16.12% on census day, and higher in all 78 municipalities. For 2006-2010 it is 16.76% against 15.91%, higher in 51 of the 78. The census records vacancy on April 1; the survey records it when each home is interviewed over five years. The Census Bureau advises against comparing the two, so compare each source only with itself.

For 2020 the vacant count behind this rate carries small privacy noise (see housing.census_vacant_units), so the 2020 rate is not exact, most of all in small municipalities. Its denominator, the total number of housing units, is exact.
Vacant includes homes for rent or sale, seasonal homes and homes empty for other reasons. It is not an abandonment rate, and it does not measure how many homes are available to residents.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.
Only two years exist (2010 and 2020).
housing.census_vacancy_pct.source_detail: Census Bureau Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) redistricting files for Puerto Rico, table H1 (housing occupancy): census_2010/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Puerto_Rico/pr2010.pl.zip and programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Puerto_Rico/pr2020.pl.zip, at www2.census.gov. On privacy noise: Census Bureau, Disclosure Avoidance for the Demographic and Housing Characteristics File (DHC) and Guidance for Data Users, 2020 Census Brief C2020BR-08 (August 2024).

housing.vacancy_pct.plain: Out of every 100 homes, how many are empty, estimated from a 5-year survey. Empty homes include homes for rent or sale, seasonal homes and abandoned homes. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.vacancy_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 viviendas, cuántas están desocupadas, según el estimado de una encuesta de 5 años. Las viviendas desocupadas incluyen las que están en alquiler o en venta, las de temporada y las abandonadas. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.vacancy_pct.definition: Vacant housing units divided by all housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) tables B25002 and B25001.
housing.vacancy_pct.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25002 cell 003 (vacant) / B25001 cell 001 (all housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 21.0% with a margin of ±0.2 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
housing.vacancy_pct.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide rate is 16.76% in 2006-2010, peaks at 23.59% in 2015-2019 and is 21.02% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.22 percentage points). In 2020-2024 it runs from 8.94% (Florida) to 65.95% (Culebra); Vieques is at 43.22%. Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: Census day versus the survey. The census vacancy rate (housing.census_vacancy_pct) is lower: 16.12% in 2020 against 22.71% for the 2016-2020 window, and lower in all 78 municipalities. For 2010 the gap is small (15.91% against 16.76%). The census records vacancy on April 1; the survey records it when each home is interviewed during five years. The Census Bureau advises against comparing the two, so compare each source only with itself.

The rate mixes homes for rent or sale, seasonal homes and homes vacant for other reasons. It does not measure abandonment; see housing.other_vacant_pct. A vacant home is not necessarily for rent or sale, and the survey does not say whether it can be lived in. These figures do not measure how many homes are available to residents.

Small places swing widely: in the 2026-10 snapshot, the highest value in any window is 70.46% (Culebra, 2019-2023). In the same snapshot, 1 of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of the estimate in the 2020-2024 window (only the Housing page's full-data table shows it in italics). Treat small differences between municipalities as noise.

The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island vacancy rate in 2020-2024 is 21.02%, while the plain average of the 78 municipality rates is 22.26%.

Each window pools five years of interviews, so it does not describe conditions on one date. The windows labeled 2017 to 2021 include the 2017 hurricane season, and those labeled 2020 to 2024 include the pandemic years. The data alone cannot show why a figure changed.

Also published for barrios, census tracts and block groups (acs_barrio.json, acs_tract.json and acs_blockgroup.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 75% of barrios, 66% of census tracts and 93% of block groups that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.

housing.vacant_units.plain: The estimated number of homes with nobody living in them, for any reason. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.vacant_units.plain_es: El número estimado de viviendas en las que no vive nadie, por cualquier razón. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.vacant_units.definition: Housing units that are vacant, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25002. Vacant homes include homes for rent or for sale, homes rented or sold but not yet occupied, seasonal or occasional-use homes, homes for migrant workers, and homes vacant for other reasons.
housing.vacant_units.method: ACS 5-year table B25002 (Occupancy Status), cell 003 (Vacant), taken as the Census Bureau publishes it. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. housing.vacant_units.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide count rises from 246,987 in 2006-2010 to a peak of 368,182 in 2015-2019. It is 354,227 in 2016-2020 and 343,491 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 3,707). In 2020-2024, 64.8% of vacant units were 'other vacant', 22.0% were seasonal, and 13.2% were for rent, for sale, sold or rented but not yet occupied, or for migrant workers.
