The 2010 census used older methods. The files carry no margin of error.

The American Community Survey (ACS) and the census differ, and not always in the same direction. For the 2016-2020 window the survey gives 354,227 vacant units against 257,625 on census day (housing.vacant_units). For 2006-2010 it gives 246,987 against 260,415 counted on April 1, 2010. housing.owner_occupied_pct.plain: Out of every 100 homes where people live, how many are lived in by their owners. The rest are lived in by renters. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
housing.owner_occupied_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 viviendas ocupadas, cuántas ocupan sus propietarios. Las demás las ocupan inquilinos. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
housing.owner_occupied_pct.definition: Owner-occupied housing units divided by all occupied housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25003. Empty homes are not in the denominator.
housing.owner_occupied_pct.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25003 cell 002 (owner-occupied) / B25003 cell 001 (all occupied housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 67.9% with a margin of ±0.3 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. layers.public_housing.definition: public_housing.geojson: one point per development HUD geocoded to the rooftop or the ZIP+4 centroid, with name, type (public housing development or scattered-site public housing), units, municipio and geoid (the municipio's GEOID). 172 of 304 developments on 2026-10-17.
layers.public_housing.method: facilities.py keeps the developments whose LVL2KX is R (rooftop) or 4 (ZIP+4 centroid), as HUD says to map, and whose point lies within 1 km of the municipio HUD gives. The 132 others sit at the centre of a block group or tract in HUD's layer; they are counted in the municipio figures but not drawn. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js, which holds its file, colour, pop-up and note.
layers.public_housing.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Land and housing: Public housing developments). Both views draw the same points, with the same note on what is counted but not drawn and the same pop-up. Click a point for the development's name, type, municipio and source.
caveats: The point is the building with the most units; a development can spread over several blocks.
About four in ten developments are not drawn because HUD could place them only approximately; the municipio counts include them.

3D view, Layers tab: Public housing developments

facilities.ph_units.plain: How many homes the public housing developments of each municipio hold, as HUD reports them.
facilities.ph_units.plain_es: Cuántas viviendas tienen los residenciales públicos de cada municipio, según HUD.
facilities.ph_units.definition: The dwelling units of the public housing developments in the municipio (HUD's TOTAL_UNITS), occupied or vacant.
facilities.ph_units.method: facilities.py sums TOTAL_UNITS over every development of the municipio (all 304, drawn on the map or not).
facilities.ph_units.how_to_read: Puerto Rico's public housing holds 54,092 units: San Juan 18,040, Ponce 5,256, Mayagüez 3,480. Per 1,000 housing units it shows how much of a municipio's housing is public housing.
caveats: HUD's unit count includes vacant units and units being repaired.
Per 1,000 housing units uses the survey's count of housing units, an estimate with a margin of error.

conditions.chas_severe_hh.plain: How many households lack a complete kitchen or plumbing, are badly overcrowded, or pay more than half their income for housing, by HUD's count for 2016-2020; the barrio figures are the observatory's estimates.
conditions.chas_severe_hh.plain_es: Cuántos hogares no tienen cocina o plomería completa, están muy hacinados o pagan más de la mitad de su ingreso en vivienda, según el conteo de HUD para 2016-2020; las cifras por barrio son estimados del observatorio.
conditions.chas_severe_hh.definition: Households with at least one of the four severe housing problems in HUD's Comprehensive Housing Affordability Strategy (CHAS) data, 2016-2020: a home without complete kitchen facilities, without complete plumbing, with more than 1.5 people per room, or a household paying more than half of its income for housing (owners plus renters, Table 2). The barrio values are estimates spread from census tracts; the municipio values are exact sums of their tracts.
conditions.chas_severe_hh.method: conditions.py reads Table 2 of HUD's CHAS for the census tracts (households with one or more of the four severe problems, owners plus renters, and all households), adds the tracts of each municipio (exact, as tracts nest in municipios), and spreads each tract's two counts over its barrios in proportion to the 2020 housing units each barrio has in the tract (geo/crosswalk.json weights; docs/geography.md, section 4); a barrio's share is its two spread counts divided.
conditions.chas_severe_hh.how_to_read: 193,934 households in Puerto Rico (16.1%): San Juan 29,843, Carolina 12,400, Bayamón 11,630. Among barrios the largest estimate is Santurce's (about 7,500).
caveats: The barrio values are estimates: a barrio that lies in several tracts gets a blend of them, as if each tract's problems were spread like its housing units.
CHAS is a survey tabulation: the Census Bureau rounds its counts, and HUD's layer publishes no margins of error; small areas are rough.
HUD User has a newer window (2018-2022) but refuses scripted downloads; this is the newest window HUD's open data service holds.
conditions.chas_severe_hh.source_detail: HUD CHAS 2016-2020 by census tract (HUD eGIS layer ACS_5YR_ESTIMATES_CHAS_TRACT): T2_EST3 + T2_EST127 over T2_EST1

conditions.chas_severe_pct.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many lack a complete kitchen or plumbing, are badly overcrowded, or pay more than half their income for housing, by HUD's count for 2016-2020; the barrio figures are estimates.
conditions.chas_severe_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos no tienen cocina o plomería completa, están muy hacinados o pagan más de la mitad de su ingreso en vivienda, según el conteo de HUD para 2016-2020; las cifras por barrio son estimados.
conditions.chas_severe_pct.definition: The share of households with at least one of the four severe housing problems in HUD's CHAS data, 2016-2020: no complete kitchen, no complete plumbing, more than 1.5 people per room, or housing costs above half of income. The barrio values are estimates spread from census tracts; the municipio values are exact sums of their tracts.
conditions.chas_severe_pct.method: conditions.py reads Table 2 of HUD's CHAS for the census tracts (households with one or more of the four severe problems, owners plus renters, and all households), adds the tracts of each municipio (exact, as tracts nest in municipios), and spreads each tract's two counts over its barrios in proportion to the 2020 housing units each barrio has in the tract (geo/crosswalk.json weights; docs/geography.md, section 4); a barrio's share is its two spread counts divided.
conditions.chas_severe_pct.how_to_read: 16.1% in Puerto Rico; San Juan and Salinas 20.6%, Guánica 7.4%. Barrio estimates run from 3% to 31% (median 14%).
caveats: The barrio values are estimates spread from tracts, so neighbouring barrios that share a tract look alike.
No margins of error are published in HUD's layer; read small differences as noise.
conditions.chas_severe_pct.source_detail: HUD CHAS 2016-2020 by census tract (HUD eGIS): (T2_EST3 + T2_EST127) / T2_EST1

study.headline_figures.plain: The study gives four round numbers. In 2020, Puerto Rico had about 1.6 million housing units and 370,000 vacant homes. The 370,000 is not the 2020 census-day count in the observatory, which is 257,625. The study estimates 300,000 units are dilapidated or abandoned. It cites a government estimate of 20,000 new homes needed each year.
study.headline_figures.plain_es: El estudio da cuatro números redondos. En 2020, Puerto Rico tenía cerca de 1.6 millones de unidades de vivienda y 370,000 viviendas desocupadas. Las 370,000 no son el conteo del día del Censo de 2020 que usa el observatorio, que es 257,625. El estudio estima que 300,000 unidades están deterioradas o abandonadas. También cita un estimado del gobierno de que hacen falta 20,000 viviendas nuevas cada año.
study.headline_figures.definition: Four headline figures shown at the top of the Housing page and quoted in its text: housing units in 2020 (1,600,000), vacant homes in 2020 (370,000), an estimate of dilapidated or abandoned units (300,000) and the annual new-housing deficit (20,000, a government estimate). The same row on the page also shows the study's 2020 resident count of 3,285,694 (see Table 2). The Census Bureau's April 2020 count is 3,285,874, which is 180 higher (see 'Resident population').
study.headline_figures.method: Stored in housing.json under headline as printed, rounded. The page labels the first two 'Census 2020, study p.14', the third 'study p.14' and the fourth 'study, regulation brief 2024'.
study.headline_figures.how_to_read: Use them as orders of magnitude. For exact counts use the live series: census-day housing units and vacant units for 2010 and 2020, and American Community Survey (ACS) housing units and vacant units for every window.
caveats: The observatory's own 2020 census-day count is 1,598,159 housing units (rounds to 1.6 million) but 257,625 vacant units, so the study's 370,000 vacant homes does not match it. The 370,000 is close to the American Community Survey estimates of vacant units: 368,182 for the 2015-2019 window and 354,227 for 2016-2020. The page labels the figure 'Census 2020, study p.14'. Treat it as the study's figure, not as the 2020 census count.
The 300,000 abandoned or dilapidated units is an estimate, not a count. The nearest public proxy in the observatory is 'other vacant' units (219,965 in the 2016-2020 window).
The 20,000 homes a year is a government estimate cited by the study. The observatory does not hold the source, and the page labels it "study, regulation brief 2024". Cite it as the study's figure.
study.headline_figures.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). p.14 and the 'regulation brief 2024' that the page cites for the 20,000 figure (the observatory does not hold the brief). Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf

study.citation_links.method: Stored in housing.json as citation and links. The page prints citation under 'Sources and method'. The links field is not read by the page, which writes the same addresses in its own text.
study.citation_links.how_to_read: Use the citation to refer to the study. NALCAB funded the study in part through its Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development program.

study.table_10.plain: Table 10 lists six housing projects named in the 2023 study. Each uses the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and also gets money from the Community Development Block Grant for Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR), a program of the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). The projects have 851 units in four municipalities. The study estimates their cost at $242,090,072 and their CDBG-DR grants at $90,532,871.
study.table_10.definition: Table 10 of the study, one row per project: project name, municipality, type (multifamily apartments or nursing home), number of units, the groups the project serves, estimated development cost and estimated CDBG-DR grant (dollars). LIHTC is the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit; CDBG-DR is the Community Development Block Grant for Disaster Recovery, a federal HUD (US Department of Housing and Urban Development) grant. The page adds a total row and a map with one circle per municipality sized by units.
study.table_10.method: Stored in housing.json under lihtc as printed. Each row has the keys name, municipality, type, units, beneficiaries, cost and cdbg_dr. The page sums units, costs and grants for the total row. Circles on the map are placed at the center of each municipality's bounding box, not at the project sites.
study.table_10.how_to_read: Totals: 851 units, $242,090,072 estimated development cost, $90,532,871 estimated CDBG-DR grant. Three projects are multifamily apartments and three are nursing homes. Caguas and San Juan have two projects each, Humacao and Coamo one each. These are the study's estimates, not figures taken from HUD, and the observatory has not updated them. The study PDF prints this table as Table 12; this dictionary and the Housing page call it Table 10 (see the entry 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023)').
caveats: These six projects are the ones listed in the study. They are not a complete list of LIHTC or CDBG-DR housing projects in Puerto Rico, and the dollar figures are not totals for any program.
The costs and grants are estimates as printed in the study. They are not obligations or payments, and the observatory does not check them against HUD or Puerto Rico Department of Housing records.
The observatory keeps this table as published in 2023. It does not add newer projects and is not refreshed from HUD's current LIHTC database.
Locations are shown at the municipality; map circles are not the project sites.
The groups the projects serve are printed as the study describes them.

values.Nursing home: 3 projects, 359 units: Caguas 200, Humacao 90, Coamo 69. The type is as printed in the study, including for a project whose name contains 'Apartments'

study.table_11.plain: A card for any one of the 78 municipalities, based on the study's Table 11 case study of Ceiba. It lists the study's variables and the housing indicators for the selected year, with each value's rank among the 78 and a small trend line.
study.table_11.plain_es: Una tarjeta para cualquiera de los 78 municipios, basada en el estudio de caso de Ceiba de la Tabla 11 del estudio. Presenta las variables del estudio y los indicadores de vivienda del año seleccionado, con la posición de cada valor entre los 78 y una pequeña línea de tendencia.
study.table_11.definition: Table 11 of the study is a case study of Ceiba. The Housing page extends its variables to every municipality: the card labeled 'Table 11 variables' shows population, change since the 2010 census, share aged 65 and over, median age, median household income, share of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher, employment rate and poverty rate. The card layout, rank and trend lines are described in the entries 'Housing page: municipality profile' and 'Trend lines (sparklines) and their length label'.
study.table_11.method: Built in the browser from housing_series.json and municipalities.json. A rank is shown for most rows, not for the maximum affordable loan or for the households approved for housing assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Population lines run to 2025 (the latest July 1 estimate); lines from the American Community Survey (ACS) end in 2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot.
study.table_11.how_to_read: Click a label to open that dataset in full; the dialog links to the dataset's entry in this dictionary. A rank of #1 means the highest value among the 78 municipalities; whether high is good depends on the measure.
caveats: Values in one card can come from different dates and surveys, for example the July 1 population estimate beside 2020-2024 ACS values and the census-day count for residents per unit. The page prints a year beside a value only when it differs from the selected year. Dollar trends are not adjusted for inflation, and neighboring ACS windows overlap.
The FEMA row adds all disasters since 2003, so a household approved under more than one disaster is counted more than once.
The study's Table 11 is a case study of one municipality, Ceiba; the page extends its variables to every municipality and every year.

study.table_2.plain: Puerto Rico's population fell from 3,725,789 at the 2010 census to 3,285,874 at the 2020 census, a loss of 439,915 people (11.8%). The 2023 study prints 3,285,694 for 2020 (180 fewer) and a loss of 440,095; both round to 11.8%. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the page also lets you compare any two years from 2010 to 2025.
study.table_2.plain_es: La población de Puerto Rico bajó de 3,725,789 en el Censo de 2010 a 3,285,874 en el Censo de 2020, una pérdida de 439,915 personas (11.8%). El estudio de 2023 publica 3,285,694 para 2020 (180 menos) y una pérdida de 440,095; ambas cifras redondean a 11.8%. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, la página también permite comparar dos años cualesquiera de 2010 a 2025.
study.table_2.definition: The study's table of Puerto Rico's resident population at the 2010 and 2020 censuses, with the change in people and the percent change (Table 5 in the study PDF; the Housing page and this dictionary call it Table 2). On the page it has three rows: the study's figures as published; the 2010 census count and the April 2020 base as held in the observatory's data; and the Census Bureau's counts or estimates for two years you choose.
study.table_2.method: The study row is typed into site/js/housing.js as printed (3,725,789; 3,285,694; -440,095; -11.8%). The live rows read Puerto Rico's value from the population series (see 'Resident population'). Change = end value minus start value; percent change = change divided by start value, times 100.
study.table_2.how_to_read: Read the first row as the study's own numbers and the next two as the observatory's recomputation. A live row that spans 2019 and 2020 mixes two estimate bases.
caveats: The study's 2020 figure (3,285,694) is 180 people lower than the 2020 island count in the observatory's population series (3,285,874). The observatory's figure equals the island total in the Census Bureau's 2020 redistricting file (Public Law 94-171). The data do not explain the study's lower figure. The page shows both figures as their sources give them; both give a change of -11.8%. For municipalities, the series' 2020 values are the April 2020 base of the Census Bureau's Vintage 2025 estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 68 of the 78 municipal values differ from the census counts by up to 31 people, and the island total is the same. The page labels the 2020 value 'census count'.
The estimates for 2011-2019 were built on the 2010 census and never revised to the 2020 count, so the series steps in 2020. The page marks the change of base with a dashed segment.
The page labels each live value as a census count (April 1) or an estimate (July 1).

study.table_3.plain: How renter households divide into nine bands of rent as a share of income, from under 10% to 50% or more. The study found 52% of renters paying 30% or more. The page redraws it for every five-year window from 2010 to 2024; in 2020-2024 the share paying 30% or more is 50.8%.
study.table_3.plain_es: Cómo se reparten los hogares inquilinos en nueve grupos según la proporción del ingreso que va al alquiler, desde menos de 10% hasta 50% o más. El estudio encontró que 52% de los inquilinos pagaba 30% o más. La página la vuelve a trazar para cada ventana de cinco años de 2010 a 2024; en 2020-2024, la proporción que paga 30% o más es 50.8%.
study.table_3.definition: Distribution of renter households in Puerto Rico by gross rent as a percentage of household income (GRAPI), American Community Survey (ACS) table B25070, in nine bands: under 10%, 10 to 14.9%, 15 to 19.9%, 20 to 24.9%, 25 to 29.9%, 30 to 34.9%, 35 to 39.9%, 40 to 49.9% and 50% or more. Each band is a percent of renter households whose ratio can be computed. The last four bands, from 30% up, are the cost-burdened and are drawn in red.
study.table_3.method: Live version: the observatory takes the Puerto Rico row of table B25070 for each window, divides cells 2 to 10 by their sum and rounds to one decimal; the result is in housing_series.json under tables.grapi. The observatory does the same for the 2020-2024 window by summing the 78 municipalities and stores it in housing.json as grapi, and the sum of the last four bands as renters_burdened_pct. The study's own 52% is typed into the page text; the study's bands are not stored in the observatory.
study.table_3.how_to_read: The data here do not show which ACS window the study used for Tables 3 and 4; the study's 52% is shown for reference, not as a comparable window. Between the 2017-2021 and 2020-2024 windows the live share goes from 52.8% to 50.8%, but those windows share two of their five years. The bands add to 100.0% give or take 0.1 because of rounding.
caveats: The fields grapi and renters_burdened_pct in housing.json are not read by the Housing page, which draws the same figures from housing_series.json. For 2020-2024 the two sources hold identical numbers (5.0, 8.8, 11.7, 11.6, 12.1, 8.5, 6.8, 8.6, 26.9).
Households in the Census Bureau's 'Not computed' group are left out: in Puerto Rico in 2020-2024, 173,394 of 414,280 renter households (42%).
The study's published distribution is not reproduced by the page; only its headline 52% is. The 2017-2021 window gives 52.8%.
The sum of the rounded bands can differ from the cost-burdened renters series, which is computed from unrounded counts, by 0.1 point in some windows (0.2 in 2013). For 2020-2024 both give 50.8%.

The observatory does not store margins of error for this island-wide live table. The Census Bureau publishes them, and the cost-burdened renters series carries them (50.8%, ± 0.2 points in 2020-2024).

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

study.table_4.plain: How owner households with a mortgage divide into nine bands of owner costs as a share of income, from under 10% to 50% or more. The study found 38% paying 30% or more. In 2020-2024 the share is 36.4%; the page prints 36.5% beside the chart because it adds the four rounded bands.
study.table_4.plain_es: Cómo se reparten los hogares propietarios con hipoteca en nueve grupos según la proporción del ingreso que va a los costos de propiedad, desde menos de 10% hasta 50% o más. El estudio encontró que 38% pagaba 30% o más. En 2020-2024 la proporción es 36.4%; la página muestra 36.5% junto a la gráfica porque suma los cuatro grupos redondeados.
study.table_4.definition: Distribution of owner households with a mortgage in Puerto Rico by selected monthly owner costs as a percentage of household income (SMOCAPI), American Community Survey (ACS) table B25091, in the same nine bands as Table 3. Each band is a percent of owner households with a mortgage whose ratio can be computed. The last four bands, from 30% up, are the cost-burdened and are drawn in red.
study.table_4.method: Live version: the observatory takes the Puerto Rico row of table B25091, divides cells 3 to 11 by their sum and rounds to one decimal (housing_series.json, tables.smocapi). The observatory does the same for 2020-2024 by summing the 78 municipalities and stores it in housing.json as smocapi, and the sum of the last four bands as owners_burdened_pct. The study's own 38% is typed into the page text.
study.table_4.how_to_read: The study's 38% is shown for reference: the data here do not show which ACS window the study used for Tables 3 and 4. The live share is 41.3% for the 2017-2021 window and 36.4% for 2020-2024 (36.5% as the sum of the rounded bands). Owners without a mortgage are not in the table.
caveats: The live 2017-2021 value for owners with a mortgage (41.3%) does not match the study's 38%. The data here do not explain the difference or show which window the study used; the page shows both. The study's published bands are not stored in the observatory.

The two 2020-2024 figures differ by rounding: 7.4 + 5.8 + 6.8 + 16.5 = 36.5, while the unrounded share of cost-burdened owners with a mortgage is 36.43. Cite 36.4% (± 0.8 points). The chart note adds the rounded bands, so it can differ by 0.1 point from the series in other windows too.
The observatory does not store margins of error for this island-wide live table. The Census Bureau publishes them, and the series carries them (36.4%, ± 0.8 points in 2020-2024).

The fields smocapi and owners_burdened_pct in housing.json are not read by the Housing page, which draws the same figures from housing_series.json. For 2020-2024 the two sources hold identical numbers (6.7, 15.2, 16.6, 14.0, 11.0, 7.4, 5.8, 6.8, 16.5).
Owner costs include utilities and taxes, not only the mortgage payment. Households in the 'Not computed' group are left out: 4,803 of 324,311 in 2020-2024.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

study.table_6.plain: The largest 30-year home loan a Puerto Rico household could carry, by age of the householder (the person in whose name the home is owned or rented), if it spends 30% of its income on housing. For all households the study found a maximum of $80,181 on a median income of $21,967. The page repeats the arithmetic for every five-year window from 2010 to 2024.
study.table_6.plain_es: El préstamo hipotecario a 30 años más grande que podría pagar un hogar de Puerto Rico, según la edad de la jefatura del hogar (la persona a cuyo nombre está la vivienda, sea propia o alquilada), si gasta 30% de su ingreso en vivienda. Para todos los hogares, el estudio encontró un máximo de $80,181 con un ingreso mediano de $21,967. La página repite el cálculo para cada ventana de cinco años de 2010 a 2024.
study.table_6.definition: Table 6 of the study has five rows (all households and four age groups of the householder: 15-24, 25-44, 45-64, 65 and over) and five columns: the age range, the median income of the age group (dollars per year), 30% of income for housing (dollars per month), the part of that paid as principal and interest (dollars per month), and the maximum 30-year mortgage (dollars). The page shows the published table, then the same arithmetic on Census Bureau incomes for the selected window.
study.table_6.method: Published: typed into site/js/housing.js as printed. Live: the observatory reads American Community Survey (ACS) table B19049 (median household income by age of householder), cells 1 to 5 for Puerto Rico, in housing_series.json under tables.t6_income_by_age. The page then computes in the browser: housing budget = income × 0.30 / 12; principal and interest = budget × 430/549; maximum mortgage = principal and interest × (1 - (1 + r)^-360) / r with r = 0.05 / 12. The same method gives max_affordable_loan for each municipality.
study.table_6.how_to_read: Read across a row: income, then the monthly budget, then the share for the loan, then the loan. The page notes that the study puts the median value of housing units at $111,800 (study, p. 22) and most homes available at asking prices of $90,000 and up.
caveats: The five published median incomes equal the observatory's values for the 2017-2021 window (labeled 2021) in table B19049, so the study's 'US Census 2021' matches the observatory's 2017-2021 window.
The page labels the first row 'Puerto Rico avg.'; the value is the median household income of all households (table B19049, cell 1), not an average.

The study prints no interest rate. The 5% rate is inferred from the study's Puerto Rico row: $21,967 of income and an $80,181 maximum loan imply 4.994%. At exactly 5% the observatory's figures are $19 to $65 below the five printed maximums.
The 78% share for principal and interest ($430 of $549) is the study's own proportion; the rest of the budget is left for taxes, insurance and other costs.
Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window and are not adjusted across windows.
A maximum loan is a yardstick, not a lender's limit: it ignores down payments, other debts and lending rules.
The observatory does not store margins of error for the live income figures. Small groups, such as householders aged 15-24 ($7,826 in 2017-2021, $13,337 in 2020-2024), can move a lot between windows.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
study.table_6.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). Table 6 (US Census 2021). Live: US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year table B19049 (Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months by Age of Householder), cells 001-005. In the study PDF this table is numbered Table 8. study.table_7.plain: What share of Puerto Rico's owner-occupied homes belongs to householders in each of seven age groups, from under 35 to 85 and over. The householder is the person in whose name the home is owned or rented. The page draws the study's published shares next to a live recomputation from the Census Bureau for the selected window.
study.table_7.plain_es: Qué proporción de las viviendas ocupadas por sus propietarios en Puerto Rico corresponde a cada uno de siete grupos de edad de la jefatura del hogar, desde menos de 35 hasta 85 o más. La jefatura del hogar es la persona a cuyo nombre está la vivienda, sea propia o alquilada. La página muestra las proporciones que publicó el estudio junto a un recálculo en vivo con datos del Negociado del Censo para la ventana seleccionada.
study.table_7.definition: Table 7 of the study: owner-occupied housing units in Puerto Rico by age of the householder, as a percent of all owner-occupied units, in seven groups: under 35, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, 75-84 and 85 and over. The published shares are 10.7, 16.4, 18.5, 22.1, 19.5, 9.6 and 3.2 (they add to 100.0).
study.table_7.method: Published: typed into site/js/housing.js. Live: the observatory reads the owner-occupied rows of American Community Survey (ACS) table B25007 for Puerto Rico and groups the age bands (15-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, 75-84, 85 and over), then divides by all owner-occupied units and rounds to one decimal (housing_series.json, tables.t7_owner_age).
study.table_7.how_to_read: The two bars are different measurements, so do not read the gap between them as a change over time. For example, the live under-35 share is 4.5% in 2017-2021 and 5.2% in 2020-2024, against 10.7% in the study. A group with a large share has many owners of that age; it does not tell you how many people of that age own a home.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, no window from 2010 to 2024 reproduces the published shares. The published under-35 share is 10.7%, but the live share is between 4.5% and 9.3%; the published 75-84 share is 9.6%, but the live share is between 10.1% and 17.0%. The closest are the 2006-2010 and 2007-2011 windows, where every group is within 1.9 points of the published share. The data do not show which window or table the study used. Read the two as different measurements.
The first live group is 15-34; the published group is labeled 'under 35'.
Live shares can add to 99.8% or 100.1% because of rounding.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
The observatory does not store margins of error for this island-wide live table.

study.state_of_housing_2023.plain: The Housing page reproduces tables and headline figures from the Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) 2023 study 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico'. It also extends many of them to all 78 municipalities with Census Bureau data. This entry describes the data file that holds the published figures. Each table has its own entry.
study.state_of_housing_2023.plain_es: La página "Vivienda" reproduce tablas y cifras principales del estudio de 2023 de Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) "The State of Housing in Puerto Rico" (El estado de la vivienda en Puerto Rico). También extiende muchas de ellas a los 78 municipios con datos del Negociado del Censo. Esta ficha describe el archivo de datos que contiene las cifras publicadas. Cada tabla tiene su propia ficha.
study.state_of_housing_2023.definition: The file housing.json has eight top-level fields: lihtc (Table 10, six projects that use the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, LIHTC); headline (four figures); citation (the study reference); links (four web addresses); and grapi, smocapi, renters_burdened_pct and owners_burdened_pct (two island-wide cost-burden distributions and their sums, recomputed from the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 data with the method of Tables 3 and 4). Tables 2, 6 and 7 and the study's 52% and 38% cost-burden figures are typed into the page code (site/js/housing.js), not stored in a data file.
study.state_of_housing_2023.method: The observatory builds the file with each snapshot: the published figures are typed as printed; the distributions are summed from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year tables for the 78 municipalities. Live versions of Tables 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 are drawn on the page from housing_series.json.
study.state_of_housing_2023.how_to_read: Items tagged 'as published' on the Housing page come from the study; items tagged 'live' are recomputed from Census Bureau data for the selected year. Read the two as different measurements of the same topic, not as corrections of each other.
caveats: This dictionary and the Housing page number the study's tables 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11. The study PDF at the address in the source line prints different numbers for the same tables. For example, it numbers the population-change table 5 (here Table 2), the gross-rent table 6 (Table 3), the home-ownership affordability table 8 (Table 6), the owner-age table 9 (Table 7), the length-of-stay table 10 (Table 8), the top-ten short-term-rental table 11 (Table 9), the low-income housing tax credit table 12 (Table 10) and the Ceiba table 13 (Table 11).
The study was produced under the Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development planning grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders).
Cite the study for the published figures and the Census Bureau for the live ones. The Housing page gives a citation for the page itself.

municipalities.acs_year.plain: The last year of the five-year Census Bureau survey window behind the housing and household figures. A value of 2024 means the figures describe 2020 to 2024.
municipalities.acs_year.plain_es: El último año de la ventana de cinco años de la encuesta del Negociado del Censo en que se basan las cifras de vivienda y hogares. Un valor de 2024 significa que las cifras describen el período de 2020 a 2024.
municipalities.acs_year.definition: The year in which the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year window ends. ACS 5-year estimates combine survey responses collected over five calendar years, so 2024 means the window 2020-2024. Every ACS-based field in the municipality record (home values, rents, income, vacancy, cost burden, poverty, employment, education and age) describes that window. All 78 municipalities carry the same value.
municipalities.acs_year.method: Set once for the whole municipality file (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot) and copied into each municipality's record. The comparison window is set the same way (2012, meaning the 2008-2012 window) and is used only by the change fields. Both years are also written to meta.json under housing (acs_latest and acs_base).
municipalities.acs_year.how_to_read: Cite the window, not the single year: write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. A window is built from five years of responses. It is not a count taken on one date.
caveats: The map and the municipality file take the window from a setting that changes only when the observatory is rebuilt. The Housing page series looks for the newest window the Census Bureau has published. After a new window is published, the Housing page can therefore show a newer window than the map and the municipality file until the observatory is rebuilt.
Windows that end one year apart share four of their five survey years, so they are not independent. The 2008-2012 and 2020-2024 windows share none.

values.2024: The ACS 5-year window 2020-2024. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is the only value present (78 of 78 municipalities).

facilities.lihtc_units.plain: How many homes the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit projects of each municipio hold, low-income and market-rate together.
facilities.lihtc_units.definition: The housing units of the LIHTC projects in the municipio (HUD's N_UNITS).
facilities.lihtc_units.method: facilities.py reads LIHTCPUB.xlsx from the archive saved by hand (cache/facilities/lihtcpub.zip; HUD USER refuses scripts), keeps the Puerto Rico rows and places each project in the county of its 2020 census tract or, where HUD has no tract, in the municipio of the city it lists (163 of 245). Every project counts, drawn on the map or not. It sums N_UNITS.
facilities.lihtc_units.how_to_read: Puerto Rico's LIHTC projects hold 23,075 units: San Juan 5,100, Ponce 1,642, Caguas 1,297. Per 1,000 housing units it shows how much of a municipio's housing was financed with the credit.
caveats: Almost every unit in Puerto Rico's projects is a low-income unit (facilities.lihtc_li_units); the two differ only where a project mixes in market-rate units.
Where HUD has no census tract for a project (163 of 245), the project counts in the municipio of the city HUD lists, which may be a mailing city: a few projects may count in a neighbouring municipio.
9 projects are no longer monitored for the credit's rules (their affordability period ended or another reason); they still count, and their units may no longer be rent-restricted.
Per 1,000 housing units uses the survey's count of housing units, an estimate with a margin of error.
These are about a federal tax credit program. Their Spanish summaries are held for Finance and Compliance review (HANDOFF decision 21).

layers.lihtc.plain: The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit projects that HUD placed at a point, on the map, with their name, municipio, units and the year they opened.
layers.lihtc.definition: lihtc.geojson: one point per LIHTC project that HUD geocoded to a point in a 2020 census tract, with name, type, municipio, geoid (the municipio's GEOID), units, low-income units (li_units) and year placed in service (year). 67 of 245 projects in HUD's 2026-04-30 release.
layers.lihtc.method: facilities.py draws a project only where HUD placed it at a point and in a 2020 census tract and the point lies within 1 km of its municipio (67 projects). The 158 projects HUD could not place are counted in the municipio figures but not drawn. The 20 projects for people who are homeless or living with HIV (HUD's TRGT_HML and TRGT_SPC) or whose name says they are a care home (an égida, a "Hogar ...": the sensitive-place words of places_privacy.py) are counted, never drawn or named (the owner's rule on sensitive places). No address is kept. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js.
layers.lihtc.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Land and housing: Tax credit housing projects). Both views draw the same points, with the same note on what is counted but not drawn and the same pop-up. Click a point for the project's name, municipio, units, low-income units, year placed in service and source.
caveats: About two in three projects are not drawn: HUD could place them only by city. The municipio counts include them.
Projects that serve people who are homeless or living with HIV, and care homes for older adults, are never drawn or named; they are in the counts.
9 projects are no longer monitored for the credit's rules (their affordability period ended or another reason); they still count, and their units may no longer be rent-restricted.
These are about a federal tax credit program. Their Spanish summaries are held for Finance and Compliance review (HANDOFF decision 21).
